beats.intro: Module eight. [[sub]]Floating-rate notes, and the yields of short-term money market instruments.
beats.frn: A floating-rate note pays a market reference rate, plus a quoted margin. [[a]]The reference rate resets every period, so the coupon follows market rates. [[bars]]Here the quoted margin is one percent. When the reference rate moves from three percent, to three point two five, and then back down, the coupon moves with it. [[b]]Because the coupon keeps up with rates, the price stays close to par. There is much less interest rate risk than in a fixed-rate bond.
beats.margin: The required margin, or discount margin, is the spread investors demand today. It reflects the issuer's credit risk and liquidity. [[eq]]If the quoted margin equals the discount margin, the note trades at par. [[disc]]Suppose the quoted margin is one hundred basis points, but investors now demand one hundred fifty. The coupon is deficient. A two year quarterly note trades at ninety nine point oh five. [[prem]]If investors demand only sixty basis points, the coupon is generous, and the price is one hundred point seven seven. [[end]]When credit weakens, the required margin rises and the price falls. When credit improves, the price rises.
beats.market: Money market instruments have original maturities of one year or less. [[a]]Treasury bills, commercial paper, and certificates of deposit are examples. They are quoted on one of two bases. [[dr]]A discount rate basis measures the interest earned relative to the face value. [[aor]]An add-on rate basis measures it relative to the price paid, which is the amount invested. [[b]]Neither compounds interest, since the term is under a year.
beats.dr: Take a one hundred eighty day certificate of deposit, quoted at a discount rate of five point nine five percent, with a three hundred sixty day year. [[pv]]The price is the face value, times one minus days over three hundred sixty, times the discount rate. One hundred times one minus one half times five point nine five percent. That is ninety seven point oh two five. [[int]]The investor pays ninety seven point oh two five, and gets one hundred back after one hundred eighty days.
beats.aor: Now measure that return on the price paid. [[aor]]Two point nine seven five divided by ninety seven point oh two five, times three sixty over one eighty, is six point one three percent. That is the add-on rate. [[bey]]Using a three sixty five day year gives the bond equivalent yield: six point two two percent. [[cmp]]The discount rate, five point nine five, understates the return, because it divides by the face value, not by the amount invested. [[ex]]Another example. An investor pays ninety six point five million for a certificate of deposit that returns one hundred million in two hundred seventy days. The add-on rate is three point five over ninety six point five, times three sixty over two seventy. That is four point eight four percent.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]A floater pays the reference rate plus a quoted margin, and stays near par. [[w2]]A quoted margin below the discount margin means a discount. [[w3]]Money market quotes use a discount rate or an add-on rate. [[w4]]Discount rates understate returns. Convert to a bond equivalent yield to compare.
